blocks.text:
You have free time until the evening. After two days of sightseeing, you can relax before the nighttime outing.

The Sambadrome is a long parade arena. Between the grandstands runs an avenue about 700 metres long, along which samba schools proceed towards Apotheosis Square. This is a competition in which each school develops its own theme through music, costumes, floats and the arrangement of its procession.

Judges score nine elements, including composition, movement, the flag and the opening dance group. Results matter to the schools: a team at the bottom of the rankings may be relegated from the top division. Behind the exuberant celebration, therefore, lies a meticulously prepared contest.

In the stands, the audience quickly becomes part of the spectacle. Thousands of spectators join in the recurring choruses; percussion sections can be heard well before the next procession arrives; and costumes and scenery change with the theme of each school.

The Sambadrome lets you watch almost the entire parade unfold continuously. First come the drummers and opening groups, followed by the main formations and floats, before the school clears the avenue for the next one. It looks like one enormous festival, yet every part follows a strict sequence. The competition between schools gives the night its momentum, as spectators compare the themes, costumes, flags and overall movement of each procession.

Carnival tickets are included in the programme. After the parade, a transfer back to the hotel is arranged.

Carnival night is meant to be enjoyed over many hours, not as a short stage show. The samba schools pass through the Sambadrome in turn, each with its own music, colours and story. As the parade progresses, individual choruses become more familiar and viewers begin to recognise recurring elements in the performances. This is what sets the Sambadrome apart from an ordinary stage production: the audience follows a moving competition that unfolds along the entire length of the arena.
